scenario: The agent opens a messy uploaded photo/screenshot/scan packet and compares it against the user's Zillow saved homes, tour info, and market data to produce a Markdown file ranking which homes to ask the realtor about next, with a visual-evidence table, a value check, and questions to ask.
did: A correct response writes gabriela_visual_home_shop.md with a room-focused ranked shortlist, per-home visual support AND visual concern, a visual-evidence table matching each usable file to a listing with a confidence level, a reasonable-value-vs-risky-stretch value check, an Ask Maria section, and an excluded section, without messaging anyone or changing any records.
why: C10 and C12 mark a correct answer wrong: C10 hard-codes a '$185,000 zestimate' for 6704 Huebner and C12 hard-codes '$170,000' for 207 Charm, but the connected Zillow data actually says 185,500 and 170,200, so an agent that reports the true figures would be failed (every other field in those two criteria checks out). The prompt asks for both the strongest visual support AND the biggest visual concern for each home, but nothing checks the biggest-visual-concern half, and nothing checks the value section's reasonable-value-vs-risky-stretch judgment (C6 only checks that the market data is present). C16 and C17 each repeat half of what C4 already checks in the same table (C16 re-checks the listing match, C17 re-checks the confidence level), so those points get counted twice.
fix: Change C10 to 185,500 and C12 to 170,200 to match the Zillow records, add a criterion for each home's biggest visual concern and one for the reasonable-value-vs-risky-stretch judgment, and delete C16 and C17 since C4 already covers the listing match and confidence level.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: The agent reviews ten contractor documents (photos, measurements, electrical, plumbing, cabinet and countertop picks, flooring and paint specs, labor and material costs, and the contract) for a kitchen renovation and gives a blunt verdict on whether the proposal holds up or has things to push back on.

why: C20 ('kitchen_reno_review.md is created with organized analysis sections covering the full scope') leans on vague words like 'organized' and 'full scope' with no named sections or list to check against, so a grader has nothing concrete to judge. C16 (flagging the $380 plumbing materials as grossly inflated versus retail) is tagged as an instruction-following check when this pricing-overcharge analysis is really core task work, so the label is wrong. C21 also bundles several MEMORY.md log parts (reviewed, sources consulted, excluded data) into one check. The facts all check out, including the photo-based findings, so these are wording and labeling issues, not factual ones, and they stay below the fail line.

agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: The agent builds a detailed home due-diligence report for 1581 Wallingford Ave N from a walkthrough video, photos, and a scanned seller disclosure, including a frame-by-frame room walkthrough, a per-room Zillow comparison, a disclosure value list, a sorted risk matrix, three financial scenarios, a date timeline, and a Greenwood pre-approval check.
did: A correct response walks the video room by room with timestamps, maps disclosed defects to each room, lists every Yes/Don't-know disclosure item and the specific written values, builds and sorts the risk matrix, computes all three cash scenarios, and tells the user whether the Greenwood listing falls inside the pre-approval range.
why: The verdict is Non-Fail; three issues were confirmed but none flip it. First, the criterion checking the main video walkthrough (the hardest, most central deliverable) is weighted +1, while comparable video-extraction criteria are weighted +5, so its weight is set about two levels too low. Second, the prompt asks for the 'approximate' timestamp of each room, but one criterion demands the laundry room match the exact time 00:37, which would mark a faithful answer of about 0:35-0:36 wrong even though the prompt itself called the value approximate. Third, the prompt asks the agent to tell the user whether the Greenwood listing at 8234 Fremont is within their pre-approval, but no criterion checks that within/outside conclusion in the output; only a process criterion checks that Zillow was consulted. Note that a prior concern about a disclosure value (section 7.B) was withdrawn after re-reading the document at higher resolution: it really does read 'Don't know', so that criterion is correct.
fix: Raise the main video-walkthrough criterion's weight to match the other +5 video-extraction criteria; loosen the laundry-room timestamp to accept an approximate value (e.g. ~0:35) instead of pinning exactly 00:37; and add a criterion that checks the report actually states whether the Greenwood listing is inside or outside the pre-approval range.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

One criterion (weight -3) penalizes the transcription unless the misspelled word is rendered exactly as 'afried', but re-reading the handwriting at high zoom shows the student actually wrote 'ofreid' (a clear 'o', then f-r-e-i-d). The closely related transcription guard on the other paragraph is fine: the student really did write 'large' there, so that criterion's premise is correct.
fix: Fix the transcription criterion so its reference spelling matches what the student actually wrote ('ofreid'), so a faithful transcription is not penalized.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: The agent finishes the user's pottery glaze_reference.md from a studio chart, a wall photo, a recipe card, and notes, working out a 200g test batch for every chart glaze (and a full batch for floating blue) with each recipe's source and per-batch material costs plus a total, then builds glaze_flashcards.csv, makes print labels in glaze_labels.md, signs up for the Saturday wheel-throwing class, and starts a fresh MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response fills glaze_reference.md with a worked test batch and recipe source for each glaze, handles the cost question, builds the flashcards and labels, takes the right enrollment action for the class, and writes the MEMORY.md log.
why: The verdict is Non-Fail. Two issues, both small. First, the prompt says each label should show the name, what goes in it, and whether it's food-safe or display-only, but no criterion checks the 'what goes in it' (ingredients) part of the labels, even though the agent's labels do list ingredients, so a required label element goes unchecked. Second, two criteria score the same decision twice in opposite directions: positive criteria reward presenting no dollar cost (since no price list was provided), and a negative criterion (-5) penalizes any dollar cost appearing, so on the main reference file the abstain-vs-write-dollars decision gets counted twice; this is counted as one issue. Everything else checks out against the source images, and the cost criteria are correctly designed because the price list was never provided (the notes say it wasn't photographed), so any dollar figure would be unsupported.
fix: Add a criterion that checks each label lists its ingredients ('what goes in it'). For the dollar-cost checks, drop the redundant negative criterion or narrow it so it only covers cases the positive criteria don't, so the same decision isn't scored twice.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: The agent writes up a creek-health survey from a field-log video, a voice note describing the scoring protocol, and bug photos taken at each station, identifying what was netted at each station, scoring it per the voice note, computing the overall reach health rating, and saving a station-by-station record as field_survey.csv with the headline rating dropped into MEMORY.md.

The only issue is that two criteria score the same decision twice in opposite directions: a positive criterion (+5) rewards using the correct denominator of 8 stations (giving 15 / 8 = 1.875), and a negative criterion (-3) penalizes averaging over the wrong number (9 or 10 instead of 8), so the choice of denominator is scored from both sides. The overlap is only partial (the positive criterion also covers the numerator), so it counts as one issue and doesn't move the verdict. The golds are otherwise correct and match the user's two correction turns and the tool results (the station-to-photo map, the scoring protocol from the voice note, and the specimen identifications all check out).
fix: Drop the negative denominator criterion or narrow it, since the positive criterion already rewards the correct denominator and the same decision is being scored twice; this is small and the verdict stays Non-Fail.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.
